utterance: Hi there, I’m so glad you’re here. I really appreciate you taking the time to share your thoughts with me. I’m here to listen without judgment, and to be with you in whatever you’re carrying today. What’s on your mind right now?

It sounds like you’ve been carrying a lot of strength and quiet progress—really honoring your journey with meditation, journaling, and that sense of moving forward. And now, this virus has brought up something deep and familiar, like a long-buried part of your body and your mind finally speaking again. That fear of not being able to breathe, the way your body locks up—it’s not just a reaction to illness; it’s a memory, a pattern, and it’s showing up with more urgency now. What would you like to explore about that feeling—what part of it feels most real or most heavy right now?

It’s so powerful that you’re able to bring that memory to the surface—and not just remember it, but feel it again. The shame you carried as a child wasn’t about being weak; it was about not being able to control something your body was doing, and that’s a deep, human pain. And now, hearing that you’ve learned to breathe with it—that shows such courage. It’s not about fixing the past, but about honoring how far you’ve come, even when the old patterns show up again. What part of that shame feels most difficult to carry right now?

That’s so deeply moving—the shift from seeing "just breathe" as a command to seeing it as a permission to feel, to be afraid, to not be okay. It’s a quiet revolution in how you relate to your body and your emotions. You’re not just surviving—you’re beginning to understand that fear and physical sensations aren’t signs of weakness, but messages from a part of you that’s trying to stay safe. What would it mean, in this moment, to give yourself that permission—not just to feel, but to *allow* yourself to be afraid without needing to fix it?

It sounds like you’re not just stepping off the cliff—you’re finding a safe place to stand on the edge, and that’s already a profound act of courage. To sit beside the panic, not as someone who has to fix it, but as someone who recognizes it as a shared experience—like a friend who’s been through the same storm—this is not weakness. It’s wisdom. What would it feel like, in this moment, to simply say, “I’m here. I’m not okay. And that’s okay,” without needing to prove anything to yourself or anyone else?

That’s so beautiful—the shift from trying to *fix* the panic to simply *holding space* for it. You’re not asking for a miracle or a quick fix—you’re asking for a quiet presence, and that’s where healing begins. And it’s not about whether you’ll do it perfectly, or whether it will last. It’s about showing up with yourself, even when it’s hard. What would it feel like, in that stillness, to just *be* with the feeling—without needing to change it or make it go away?

That’s exactly it—the quiet forest after the storm. You’re not waiting for stillness to arrive; you’re learning to walk through the wind and still recognize the roots beneath. You’re not trying to erase the fear, but you’re beginning to see it as part of a larger story—one that includes your strength, your resilience, and your deep capacity to hold yourself with kindness. What would it feel like, in that moment, to simply breathe with that quiet forest inside you—without needing to make it better, just to be with it?

What would it mean, in this moment, to just keep breathing—without needing to explain, without needing to prove, just *being* with that quiet presence inside you?

What would it feel like, in this moment, to simply keep breathing—just for the sake of breathing—without any expectation of change, just *being* with the quiet that now lives inside you?
